newsitem.title: CHINA: China industrial output sags on overcapacity, heat.
newsitem.headline: China industrial output sags on overcapacity, heat.

text.p: China's industrial output grew by 8.4 percent year-on-year in July, far below expectations and economists said on Friday huge overcapacity and a summer heat wave were probably behind the sharp slowdown.

The 8.4 percent increase took the value of industrial output to 162.5 billion yuan ($19.6 billion) in July. But the rate of growth was down from a roaring first half performance of 11.6 percent, the State Statistical Bureau said on Friday.

The figure, which failed to meet official forecasts of 12-14 percent, surprised many economists, who said factors ranging from an unusually hot summer to industrial overcapacity and holidays over the Hong Kong handover could have caused the drop.
Light industrial output grew 8.3 percent in July while heavy industry showed growth of 8.5 percent, the figures showed.
Output of state enterprises rose 3.9 percent while output of collectives grew 7.7 percent and that of private industry rose 11.9 percent.
All those figures represented falls of 1.6 to 4.8 percentage points compared with first half performances.
The State Statistical Bureau attributed the drops to lost working days due to a record heatwave that hit much of northern China last month, an analysis with which many Chinese economists agreed.
"The most possible reason is the exceptionally hot weather," said Sheng Hong, an economist with the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
"I don't think there are any other factors that could have affected industrial growth because the overall situation of the industrial economy is not bad," Sheng said.

The July 1 handover of Hong Kong to Chinese rule affected industrial output because a jubilant Beijing granted workers two extra days of holiday, said Ken Chan, an economist with Nikko Securities in Hong Kong.
But other economists said industrial overcapacity and rising inventories were bigger factors dragging down growth.

Although the sales rate of industrial goods inched up 0.51 percentage points in July to 96.34 percent, many businesses were still trying to clean out big stockpiles, said Qu Hongbin, chief economist with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in Hong Kong.
"The effective demand in China is not as strong as many people thought," Qu said. "They have to wait until market conditions improve."
Industrial overcapacity had also limited growth, giving factories little incentive to boost output and discouraging newcomers from jumping into a saturated market, economists said.
Makers of consumer goods such as televisions and cars have been forced to slash prices in recent months as competition heated up amid huge overcapacity.
China could seek to spur industrial growth by ecnouraging exports, but the 25 percent export growth rate of the past few months would be hard to beat, Qu said.
"Any growth rate higher than that will be difficult for China to achieve, and domestic demand I don't expect to pick up over the next six to eight months," he said.
Economists said they saw growth picking up later in the year if enterprises expanded production amid cooler weather and after slashing inventories.

"I don't expect this eight percent to last for the rest of the year," Qu said. "The output number may come back to some level around 10 or 11 percent, but won't compare to last year's level (of 13.1 percent)."
